items.title: Ask Pinstripe Alley: Yankees mailbag questions request
items.author: Madison Pavich
items.content:
The Yankees completed their homestand this weekend with about as good of a result as you could ask for. After dropping two of three to Houston and getting just one run scored in the finale of that series, Friday’s 1-0 nailbiter of a win against Boston and subsequent shutout loss to them on the first game of a doubleheader on Saturday brought back concerns of their stagnant offense. However, they ripped through the final two games, scoring nine in the nightcap to split the doubleheader before blasting their way to 16 runs in the finale on Sunday to take the series and the season record against Boston. They now stand four games up on the Red Sox in the standings, but with that tiebreaker in hand they’ve got an extra game of protection should these two teams remain in the top Wild Card slots and face off to start October.

The final month of the season is now in front of them, and they’ve got both a sizeable gap on Boston to uphold while also facing a nearly-identical gap between them and Tampa Bay for first place. Their penultimate series of the season lines them up to deal with that problem head-on, but if the deficit isn’t more than a game or two by then the odds of totally flipping the standings are negligible. Is the offensive eruption they had this weekend a sign of the lineup finally clicking, or will the droughts keep popping up? Was Will Warren’s performance in the finale the best start he’s had in his career, and can he follow it up with more down the stretch? How much are you expecting from Aaron Judge as he gears up to jump straight back into an MLB lineup without rehab games? If you have questions like these, or anything else on your mind, send ‘em in for a chance to be featured in our Yankees mailbag.

Answers will run on Friday afternoon. All questions received by the night of September 3rd will be considered. You can leave your submissions in the comment section below or by e-mail to pinstripealleyblog [at] gmail [dot] com.

items.title: Yankees claim reliever John Schreiber off waivers from Royals
items.author: Dani Mohr
items.content:
Days after hitting the waiver wire, reliever John Schreiber is making a new home in the Bronx.

The 32-year-old right-hander joins the Yankees bullpen with a 3.65 ERA in 55 appearances with Kansas City this season. Through 49.1 innings pitched, however, Schreiber’s strikeout (17.7 percent) and walk (10.8 percent) numbers raise some questions that aren’t exactly reassuring for the September playoff push.

This move will hopefully allow relievers David Bednar, Brent Headrick, and Paul Blackburn to take some much-needed rest after exhausting their efforts in the last few series against the Blue Jays, Astros, and Red Sox.

Schreiber first went to Kansas City in 2024 in a trade with the Red Sox for David Sandlin. He initially made his MLB debut with the Tigers in 2019 and spent two seasons with the team before he was claimed by Boston.

With the postseason looming, this move has the potential to work out well for the Yankees after losing both Fernando Cruz and Ryan Weathers to the IL. Accompanied by fellow new additions Michael Fulmer and Luis Gil, who was most recently called up on Sunday, Schreiber is an addition that can help the Yankees’ bullpen shut down any offense.

items.title: On MLB’s most recent CBA proposals
items.author: John Griffin
items.content:
This past Thursday, Major League Baseball made its latest round of proposals to the Players’ Association, this type focusing on so-called “roster stability.” Claiming that roster churn during both the season and offseason makes it difficult for fans to keep track of which players are currently on the roster, the league proposed shrinking the offseason to a three-week period in December, instituting weekly rosters, and dropping the amount of times a player can be optioned to the minors during a season from five to four. Between these proposals and the salary cap — to which these proposals are tied — the league believes that their proposal will succeed at “creating more stability in rosters, getting the best players to the Major Leagues more quickly, and accelerating the pace of the offseason.”

If you read any of my work from the previous CBA negotiations, when I outlined all the ways that the league’s proposals last time were rooted in attempts to reduce player salaries and increase ownership control over the game, you wouldn’t be surprised to learn that I see the league’s latest pitch to be completely self-serving. By reducing the offseason to a few short weeks in December, the league wants a free agent frenzy like you see in the NFL and NBA…but in truth, the deadline will give teams extra leverage, because, in the words of FanGraphs’ Michael Baumann, “players would be forced to sign before Christmas or risk remaining unemployed until the start of spring training.” Weekly rosters will limit roster turnover, yes, but it will also limit the amount of players who will sit on their team’s version of the Scranton Shuttle, slowly earning service time over the course of the season, increasing team control over bottom-of-the-roster types. And, of course, when all of these are tied to a salary cap, you’re making player contracts and roster spots even more of a zero-sum game than they already are.

That being said, there is the core of a good idea here: the inclusion of “quiet periods” in the offseason. At the moment, the Major League Baseball offseason calendar begins immediately after the end of the World Series. The very next day, all players whose contracts have expired become free agents, although they are unable to sign with other teams until the fifth day after the World Series. Practically, this makes this five-day period an exclusive window to re-sign free agents, during which time teams must extend qualifying offers and either accept or reject team options, and players must exercise opt-outs (or not). Oh, and during this time, the trade market opens back up too.

Compared to other sports, this is a very short window between the end of the championship and the formal start of the offseason. To put that in perspective, let’s take a look at the timelines that the NFL and NBA use.

On February 14, 2027, Super Bowl LXI will be played. The new league year will not begin until almost a month later, on March 9, 2027. In between these two dates, no transactions can officially be completed (while some trades get negotiated and reported on, they cannot officially take place until the start of the new league year), giving teams a period of time after the championship to reflect on the past season and make a plan of action for the offseason.

Okay, but the Super Bowl is a one-day affair, so that’s not a perfect one-to-one comparison. What about another sport whose championship can end over a period of time, such as the NBA? Well, the Knicks clinched their first NBA Finals championship on June 13th. The NBA Draft — which is, officially, the last event of the 2025-2026 season, even if everyone thinks of it as the start of the near year — occurred ten days later. The new league year, and thus free agency and the trade market, didn’t open up until July 6th. It’s not quite as much of a breather between the championship and the offseason as the NFL, but it does give more time than we get in baseball.

According to Major League Baseball’s pitch, the first five days after the World Series would remain exactly the same, but free agency would not begin until the Winter Meetings in December. On December 21st, free agency would slam shut and a trade moratorium would commence, and neither would open again until the the start of spring training in February. This essentially institutionalizes what already happens on the front end — very few transactions occur during the month of November — guarantees that a lot of business happens at the Winter Meetings (which, with the exception of the Shohei Ohtani sweepstakes, generally happens anyway), and turns January, when the NFL playoffs dominate the sports news cycle, into a dead period. Despite the league’s insistence, this proposal doesn’t exactly transform the offseason; it simply guarantees that it moves at the beat of the league’s drums.

If the league genuinely wants to fix the offseason, there’s quite a bit of low-hanging fruit. The current offseason structure is an amalgamation of almost 200 years of evolution, from the player-led amateur clubs of the mid-19th century through today. Free agency begins immediately after the World Series, but the meetings during which their agents are most likely to meet with teams doesn’t occur until six weeks later. Arbitration-eligible players are tendered contracts in November whose values are not known until January. Nobody creating a league from scratch would structure their offseason like this. In fact, the sports videogame franchise that attempts to simulate baseball front offices, , employs its own offseason calendar because the real one is so convoluted that the computer-controlled teams would struggle with it.

Ironically, ’s model could supply some inspiration to reform the offseason calendar. When using default settings, players don’t file for free agency until a few weeks after the end of the World Series, which is also the same time as the salary arbitration deadline. This is, of course, done for gameplay considerations, ensuring that both human- and computer-controlled teams know where their budgets stand when free agency begins. The same logic, though, applies to real life. Finishing salary arbitration before free agency opens would give front offices some certainty for embarking on their winter plans, and the fact that it would delay the opening of free agency until, say, late November would turn the Winter Meetings into the free agent marquee event they want it to be, just without the unnatural “hurry up and wait” approach of the league’s proposal.

The second “frozen zone” of MLB’s proposal is also, in theory, a good idea — so long as it’s limited to just being a holiday break, not an offseason deadline. The period between Christmas and New Year’s is arguably the quietest part of the baseball calendar, because let’s be honest, everybody wants to spend the holidays with their families, not working. Well, everybody except AJ Preller, apparently. MLB Executive Burner (who is often speculated to be Mike Elias) said in response on Twitter:

Even beyond these practical reasons for the delayed start to free agency, it’s also a much more aesthetically pleasing offseason. Think back to the end of the 2024 season. Twenty-four hours after the final out of the World Series, before we even had a chance to think about starting our end-of-season coverage here on Pinstripe Alley, the baseball world had already turned the page and started the offseason. Juan Soto, Alex Verdugo, Anthony Rizzo, Gleyber Torres, and Gerrit Cole (who, you may recall, temporarily exercised his opt-out that winter before the Yankees called his bluff) fell off the active roster and were purged from the Yankees’ website…and that would’ve happened even if the team won. Can you imagine if Mitchell Robinson had gone down the Canyon of Heroes celebrating the Knicks championship while under contract with the Boston Celtics? Theoretically, that’s possible in baseball — highly unlikely, considering cities try not to wait before having their parade, but still possible. And let’s be honest, who really wants to check MLB Trade Rumors while watching their nieces and nephews open up presents from Santa on Christmas morning?

Of course, Major League Baseball may have stumbled on some really good ideas, but at the end of the day, do we actually trust that they’ll pursue the good ideas in lieu of chasing a quick buck. With Rob Manfred in charge, the man who — in the words of Keith Law — finds a golden egg and sees only a goose that needs to be killed, I wouldn’t count on it.

items.title: The Yankees Birthday Series, presented by Pinstripe Alley
items.author: Andrew Mearns
items.content:
During my tenure at Pinstripe Alley—hell, during my entire time as a baseball fan—I’ve never been shy about delving into the team’s history and exploring the lives of its long roll call of players, both incredible and regrettable. We provide plenty of other coverage on the current-day activities of the teams, so I like having one spot per day on the schedule to open the ol’ books and tell a story.

Whether it’s remembering championship teams, Top 100 players, or notable free agent signings, there’s always something out there to explore. For the pastthreeyears, we’ve celebrated the 25th anniversary of the 1998-2000 Yankees dynasty by doing a diary on all their regular season and playoff activity. The final pages were written this past October, so it’s time for a new daily project.

With that in mind, we’ll ring in the new year by beginning the Yankees Birthdays series. Every day in 2026, we’ll have a new Yankees figure to discuss whose birthday happened to fall on that day. Some days will feature far more famous stars than others! But that just adds to the challenge and our interest in the exercise. As a spoiler for today, that’s exactly what you’ll see soon for January 1st.

Happy new year and happy 365 days of Yankees birthdays!

items.title: Yankees Birthday of the Day: Claudell Washington
items.author: Kevin Winterhalt
items.content:
Claudell Washington had a darn fine major league career, sticking around for 17 seasons, making a couple of All-Star appearances. More notably, he was part of the World Series champion Oakland Athletics in his rookie season, the third title in a row for the mighty A’s. I can only imagine what that does to the psyche. Unfortunately for Washington, that was his only championship ring.

His time as a Yankee accounts for a fraction of his overall career, playing all or part of four seasons in pinstripes. But in a historical quirk, Washington is a surprisingly significant part of Yankee lore.

: Claudell Washington: August 31, 1954 (Los Angeles CA): June 10, 2020 (Orinda, CA): 1986-1988, 1990

Washington’s career got off to quite the start. As mentioned, the rookie outfielder won a World Series with Oakland in 1974, having just turned 20 years old that August. For his part, though not an everyday starter in the postseason, Washington rose to the moment. He went 7-for-18 in his first taste of playoff baseball.

The next season was the finest of his career by almost any metric. He earned his first All-Star Game nod and the As made another trip to the playoffs, though they fell three games to one to Boston. That was the last time Washington played October baseball for a while.

After one more season in Oakland, Washington bounced around, playing for Texas, the White Sox, the Mets, and the Braves between 1977 and 1985. Unfortunately for him, he’s perhaps best known during that time for a 1985 arrest for possession of marijuana and cocaine. He did permanently etch his name in baseball lore in 1980, however. Washington notched a three-homer game in 1979 for the White Sox. The next season, he repeated the feat, this time for the Mets. By doing so, he became the third man to accomplish that feat in both leagues, joining Babe Ruth and Johnny Mize.

In June 1986, Atlanta dealt him to the Yankees in a trade that saw Ken Griffey, Sr. head to the Braves. Washington re-signed in the Bronx that offseason and was a productive member of the lineup for the next couple years, batting .296/.340/.433 with 39 doubles, 20 homers, 25 stolen bases, and a 111 OPS+ across 228 games.

At the old Metrodome in Minnesota on April 20, 1988, Washington hit the 10,000 home run in franchise history, making the Yanks the first club to reach that milestone — no small feat considering how much older plenty of the National League teams are in comparison.

That wasn’t his only highlight of the 1988 campaign, either. On September 11th, Washington stepped up to bat against former MVP Willie Hernandez. The Tigers and Yankees endured a marathon in the Bronx, with both sides going scoreless for 10 consecutive innings from the eighth through the 17th. Detroit had finally broken through in the top of the 18th on an RBI single from future Diamondbacks skipper Torey Lovullo.

But Hernandez was tired in his third inning of work and walked Rickey Henderson to lead off the home half. That made Rickey the tying run at first base, always a dangerous proposition. Washington was next up though, and he just ended it right then and there. In terms of innings, it was the latest walk-off homer in Yankees history.

Washington left New York for the Angels after the 1988 season. If Washington was to be believed, the sticking point was $200,000. He told the :

”I was playing with five or six potential Hall of Famers. That’s rare. All I wanted was a $200,000 buyout for an option year and they wouldn’t agree to it. That’s what it was: $200,000.”

In the end, he returned to New York, albeit more than a year later. In April 1990, the Angels dealt Washington back to the Yanks, who released him that October after 33 unproductive games for the last-place club. It marked the end of his career.

Washington died in June 2020. He had suffered from prostate cancer since 2017.

Claudell Washington’s tenure in New York was brief. But he tallied a couple of the more historic homers in franchise history, too. He was also, according to reporter Murray Chass, one of the aforementioned Rickey Henderson’s favorite teammates with the Yankees. Happy heavenly birthday, Claudell Washington!

See more of the “Yankees Birthday of the Day” series here.

items.title: Yankees Rivalry Roundup: Tampa wins again; El Gary goes yard for the 200th time
items.author: Kevin Winterhalt
items.content:
After the Yanks bludgeoned Boston Sunday, it was time to scoreboard watch. Most notably, could the Padres do us all a solid and knock off the Rays? To the surprise of absolutely no one, the answer was no. So while the Yankees put more distance between themselves and Boston and clinched the season series between the two eternal rivals, there was no ground gained on Tampa.

Elsewhere, a former Baby Bomber achieved a career milestone while a future Hall of Fame hurler further stated his Cooperstown case.

Tampa Bay Rays (82-54) 5, San Diego Padres (72-65) 4 (F/11)

Bloody Devil Magic. The Padres looked to have this game wrapped up, with a ninth-inning lead and Mason Miller on the mound. Since joining the Padres last season, the All-World closer had surrendered precisely two home runs over 79.2 frames as he took the mound Sunday. So, of course he promptly gave up a game-tying two-run blast to Johnny DeLuca. But hold on. This was no run of the mill home run.

As I said, bloody Devil Magic. After a scoreless 10th, the Dads took a lead in the 11th. But it was all for naught. A DeLuca ground ball to Xander Bogaerts ended in an error and re-tied the game. Then, former Yankee farmhand Jorge Mateo ended it with a walk-off single.

Chicago White Sox (72-64) 1, Minnesota Twins (65-72) 5: For all intents and purposes, this one was over before the opening frame came to a close. Minnesota plated three in the home first, more than enough for starter Zebby Matthews. Matthews took a shutout into the ninth before the Pale Hose managed to scrape across a run. Matthews’ day ended with 8.1 innings allowing that lone run. That continues a strong run, as he has pitched to a 3.21 ERA in his last seven outings, averaging 6 IP/start.

Houston Astros (69-68) 6, New York Mets (61-76) 3: LaMonte Wade, Jr. was Sunday’s hero for Houston. His pinch-hit two-run home run gave the Astros a lead they never surrendered. The victory keeps H-town two games ahead of their intra-state rival Rangers.

Texas Rangers (67-70) 7, Milwaukee Brewers (85-52) 4: Texas won Sunday to stay in the mix in the AL West and Wild-Card races. But for Yankees fans, Gary Sánchez was the story. The Kraken clubbed the 200th home run of his career, 138 of which came in pinstripes, in defeat. Sigh. We’ll always have the second half of 2016.

Cleveland Guardians (69-68) 11, Kansas City Royals (62-76) 1: Welcome to the José Ramírez Show. The Cleveland third baseman has been mired in his worst offensive season since 2015. Not Sunday, however. Ramírez homered and drove in four as the 3-4-5 batters for Cleveland combined to plate 10 runs.

-69) , Athletics (53-) 5: Gunnar Henderson has had a rough 2026. But on Sunday, he looked every bit the young superstar. Four hits, two of which left the yard, led to three runs scored and five batted in as the Os swept the As.

Toronto Blue Jays (68-70) 7, Seattle Mariners (64-73) 0: For one day at least, Max Scherzer was “Mad Max” again. While tossing seven frames of one-hit shutout ball, Scherzer punched out 10. The last of those moved him ahead of Gaylord Perry for ninth all-time on the career strikeout list.

items.title: New York Yankees vs. Los Angeles Angels: Series Preview
items.author: Joshua Diemert
items.content:
After a hard-fought and ultimately successful four-game series with the Red Sox, winning three of four and securing the tiebreaker between the two teams, the Yankees head west to take on the dreadful Angels. Perhaps the most dysfunctional organization in baseball, which is saying something, Arte Moreno already cleaned house earlier this year firing longtime GM Perry Minasian, but the problem may be Moreno himself. On pace to lose 101 games, the Angels have wasted one of the likely last strong years of Mike Trout’s career, as well as a season where a number of pitchers proved themselves valuable.

All of this is to say, this isn’t a trap series exactly, but it’s almost a trap series. After the endorphins of a good series against Boston wear off, the Angels are still a major league team, and anyone can beat anyone two out of three times. This is a series the Yankees should win, almost have to win to keep up the pressure on the Rays, but we’ve seen how those kind of circumstances can go awry in the past.

vs. Mitch Farris (9:38pm Eastern)

With Ryan Weathers on the IL, ERC will get at least two more chances to show off within the MLB rotation, his fourth stint with the team this year. His last outing was the longest of his young big league career, throwing six innings against the hated Astros, allowing a trio of runs and striking out a batter per inning. He looks to be beginning to find a handle on his pitch mix — the stuff has popped since his debut, but he’s shown a struggle with his control that seems to be improving. This is a pretty ideal setup for a young pitcher, as the Angels boast the third-worst offense in baseball.

The Angels are a fascinating group because a man named Mitch Farris is expected to get the ball on Monday night. Farris has not started a game for the Angels this year, used in a variety of bullpen roles, and will be called on to give an abbreviated beginning. The left-hander features a slowwwwwww changeup that’s probably his best offering, but his fastball gets clobbered and the Yankees are in a bit of a lefty-slugging mood lately.

Tuesday — Gerrit Cole vs. Walbert Ureña (9:38pm Eastern)

In a season with so many incredible pitching stories, Gerrit Cole’s may be the second-most impressive after only Cam Schlittler. The veteran has hardly missed a beat in coming off of Tommy John surgery, already eclipsing his innings total from the 2024 season, throwing the ball harder than that year as well. His 3.19 ERA is backstopped well by a 3.37 FIP, and even if he’s slightly overperforming his HR-allowed baseline, what you’ve seen from Cole this year should mostly be believed.

Walbert Ureña has looked like a real pitcher in his rookie season, throwing 118 innings of 2.94 ERA that might just net him some downballot Rookie of the Year votes if anyone is paying attention to Orange County. He doesn’t strike many out, and he walks a few too many, but in a ballpark that surrenders a lot of home runs he keeps it in the yard.

Wednesday — Cam Schlittler vs. Grayson Rodriguez (9:38pm Eastern)

It’s #CamBumpDay and with Cam tied with Dylan Cease at 5.1 fWAR, a big performance against a bad team could give him a slight edge in a dynamite AL Cy Young race. The added benefit for Cam is the game coming on the road, where eagle-eyed viewers have noticed a bit of a home/road split for the young righty:

On paper, everything is set up for the youngster to pull just a bit ahead of Cease, but execution is still everything in this game.

Rodriguez, the white-hot hope of the rebuilding Baltimore Orioles’ rotation, has flatlined in his first season with LA. Worth just half a win, a 6.04 ERA actually belies a FIP that’s stronger, but Grayson finds himself with poor results with an organization not known for improving performance, whistling past the proverbial baseball graveyard.

items.title: Today on Pinstripe Alley – 8/31/26
items.author: Jake Devin
items.content:
The Yankees are heading West, and they do so after a pretty cathartic weekend. They played four games against their hated rivals with playoff seeding at stake, and after a tense first couple of matchups, New York awakened in the final two contests, unloading on the Red Sox for a combined 25 runs across two games. It was a triumphant showing, and on the heels of the news that Aaron Judge will traveling with the team to Anaheim, things are looking up.

There’s a real chance here to keep the momentum going, with the Yankees taking on the Angels for three starting tonight. Josh will have you covered with the series preview this morning. Later, Kevin recaps Sunday in the American League, and also profiles Claudell Washington as part of our Yankee Birthday series. And in the afternoon, John discusses the most recent CBA proposals that have been reported.

New York Yankees at Los Angeles Angels

Venue: Angel Stadium, Anaheim, CA

1. What was your biggest positive takeaway from this weekend’s series win over Boston?

2. Now that Aaron Judge is traveling with the team to California to ramp up on-field activities, do you expect him to be activated for the next homestand?

items.title: Yankees news: Aaron Judge to travel with Yankees on West Coast trip
items.author: Jake Devin
items.content:
MLB.com | Bryan Hoch: The Yankees are off to the West Coast, and Aaron Judge is coming with them. The plan is for Judge to really start ramping up this week, including taking on-field batting practice. “Hopefully out there, he’ll start to get on velocity and things like that,” Aaron Boone said. “He’ll be part of the pregame stuff and just get more entrenched into getting ready to come back.” Though it’d be a major surprise to see Judge play during this trip, it seems possible that the team’s next homestand could see him return.

ESPN | Jorge Castillo: Rookie George Lombard Jr. left Saturday night’s game after tweaking his knee, and though he’s avoided any structural damage, he’s could still hit the injured list. “It feels fine,” Lombard said. “It’s definitely better than yesterday. It felt a little stiff, and there’s still a little soreness, a little inflammation in there, but not terrible.” Jose Caballero, who was the starting shortstop for the first several weeks of the season, started at short on Sunday. Anthony Volpe is also biding his time at Triple-A, with the erstwhile starter at short having moved around the infield in the last month, taking several starts at second, and even starting at third over the weekend.

New York Post | Mark W. Sanchez: The Yankees called up Luis Gil yesterday, the 2024 AL Rookie of the Year giving the club a fresh arm and taking Yerry De los Santos’ spot on the roster. Things are set up for the Yankees to have something of a bullpen audition in September, as there’s plenty of room in Aaron Boone’s Circle of Trust. Gil could toss his name into the mix, as could Clarke Schmidt, who made a rehab appearance over the weekend. Most everything is up for grabs beyond David Bednar, Brent Headrick and Paul Blackburn, so anyone that performs well over the season’s final month could become a factor come October.
